title: Token-Based Authentication
description: Use personal access tokens and fine-grained tokens for secure Git authentication over HTTPS.

data.text: Personal access tokens (PATs) replace passwords for Git HTTPS authentication. They provide granular permissions, can be revoked without changing your password, and work with two-factor authentication. GitHub's fine-grained tokens provide even more precise control over repository access.
Generate a PAT in your GitHub account settings. Choose the classic token for broad compatibility or the fine-grained token for precise permissions.

data.title: Create a fine-grained personal access token
data.code:
# GitHub: Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens → Fine-grained tokens

# Create a new token with:
# - Name: "Development token"
# - Expiration: 90 days (or custom)
# - Repository access: Select repositories
# - Permissions:
#   - Contents: Read and write
#   - Metadata: Read
#   - Pull requests: Read and write

# Copy the token immediately — you cannot view it again

# Use the token as your password:
git clone https://github.com/your-username/project.git
Username: your-username
Password: ghp_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx

# Or store in Git credential manager
git config --global credential.helper manager-core
# (prompts once, then stores securely)

data.text: In CI, store tokens as encrypted secrets. Use the secret in your workflow to authenticate push operations or access private repositories.

data.title: Use a token in GitHub Actions
data.code:
# .github/workflows/deploy.yml
- name: Checkout
  uses: actions/checkout@v4
  with:
    token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

# For private repositories or push operations:
- name: Push changes
  run: |
    git config user.name "GitHub Actions"
    git config user.email "actions@github.com"
    git remote set-url origin https://x-access-token:${{ secrets.PERSONAL_TOKEN }}@github.com/owner/repo.git
    git push origin main
  env:
    PERSONAL_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.PERSONAL_TOKEN }}

items: **Use fine-grained tokens**: Grant only the permissions needed for the task
**Set expiration**: Tokens should expire after 90 days or less
**Store in secrets**: Never hardcode tokens in scripts or commit them to Git
**Revoke when done**: Delete tokens when they are no longer needed
**Use different tokens**: Use separate tokens for development and CI

data.title: If a token is exposed, revoke it immediately
data.text: A leaked token gives anyone who has it full access to the repositories and permissions you granted. Revoke it in GitHub Settings immediately and create a new one.
Storing tokens securely on your machine
Use the Git credential manager to store tokens securely. Never hardcode tokens in scripts or environment variables that persist in your shell history.

data.title: Configure Git credential manager
data.code:
# Configure Git to use the credential manager
git config --global credential.helper manager-core

# On Linux, you may need to install it first:
# sudo apt-get install libsecret-1-dev
# git-credential-libsecret

# The next time you enter a token:
git clone https://github.com/username/project.git
Username: username
Password: ghp_xxxxxxxxxxxx

# The credential manager stores the token securely
# and automatically provides it for future operations

data.text: Classic tokens (ghp_...) have broad scopes (repo, workflow, etc.). Fine-grained tokens (github_pat_...) allow you to select specific repositories and granular permissions. Use fine-grained tokens for new integrations.

data.title: Fine-grained token permissions
data.code:
# Fine-grained token example permissions:
# - Repository: Read (to clone)
# - Contents: Read and write (to push)
# - Pull requests: Read (to create PRs)
# - Workflows: Read (to trigger workflows)

# Fine-grained tokens are tied to specific repositories
# and cannot access all repositories like classic tokens.

items.question: Can I use SSH instead of HTTPS with tokens?
items.answer: No. SSH uses key-based authentication. Tokens are for HTTPS only. Use SSH keys for SSH authentication.

items.question: Do tokens work with two-factor authentication?
items.answer: Yes. Tokens are the recommended way to authenticate when 2FA is enabled. Passwords do not work with 2FA.

items.question: How do I revoke a token?
items.answer: Revoke tokens in GitHub Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens. Find the token and click 'Revoke'.

items.question: Can I see when a token was last used?
items.answer: Yes. GitHub shows the last used date for each token in the token settings. Use this to identify unused tokens for revocation.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Use personal access tokens for HTTPS authentication
Prefer fine-grained tokens (github_pat_) over classic tokens (ghp_)
Store tokens in GitHub Secrets or the Git credential manager
Set token expiration and revoke when no longer needed
Different tokens for development and CI environments
